extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in the history of censorship and American social/legal history
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article describing the history, actions, and legal/political role of the New York Society for the Suppression of Vice (NYSSV), including examples of works and behaviours it targeted and the legal mechanisms it used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission: supervising the morality of the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society was 'dedicated to supervising the morality of the public' and better remembered for opposition to literary works while also monitoring newsstands and periodicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames the NYSSV's purpose broadly as enforcing public morality through scrutiny of publications and public displays; examples include campaigns against books, plays, magazines and newsstand materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor compliance with state laws and work with courts/DA
rubrics_metrics.description: The NYSSV's specific mission was 'to monitor compliance with state laws and work with the courts and district attorneys in bringing offenders to justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the operational standard: detect alleged violations of law and pursue formal legal action rather than purely social pressure; they also 'pushed for additional laws against perceived immoral conduct.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Charter-granted powers: search, seizure, and arrest; share of fines
rubrics_metrics.description: When chartered by the New York state legislature (May 1873) the society was 'granted its agents the powers of search, seizure, and arrest, and awarded the society half of all fines levied in resulting cases.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural/authority standard describing the legal powers and financial incentives that authorized and motivated enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for action: 'violating public decency'
rubrics_metrics.description: The society pursued arrests and prosecutions for 'violating public decency' (example: encouraged authorities to arrest Olga Nethersole and others over the play Sapho in 1900).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses the phrase 'violating public decency' as an operational criterion applied to theatre and other public performances; cases could result in trial even if defendants were later found innocent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity as basis for seizure, ban, or prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The NYSSV repeatedly targeted materials it labeled 'obscene', resulting in seizures, trials, bans and prosecutions (examples include Ulysses, Jurgen, Lady Chatterley's Lover, works by Oscar Wilde and others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenity served as the primary normative/legal standard for many actions: books and magazines deemed 'obscene' were seized, publishing/printing materials confiscated, and distribution/possession prosecuted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prurient or sensuous descriptions considered objectionable
rubrics_metrics.description: The page quotes criticism that newspapers could 'flaunt criminal advertisements, or prurient or sensuous descriptions' and that such content was targeted by the Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prurient/sensuous descriptions — even in context of reporting — were characterized as morally harmful and thus candidates for suppression; this helps define the Society's scope beyond explicit pornographic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual explicitness (e.g., depiction of masturbation) grounds for obscenity charges
rubrics_metrics.description: The serialization in The Little Review of a passage of Ulysses 'dealing with the main character masturbating' led the NYSSV to attempt to keep the book out of the U.S.; at trial the magazine was declared obscene and Ulysses was banned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual acts described or depicted explicitly were treated as obscene content justifying legal action and importation/sale bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depictions of adultery and homosexuality labeled obscene
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society encouraged the arrest of a bookseller for selling Mademoiselle de Maupin, 'which depicted adultery and homosexuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals of adultery and homosexuality were treated as potentially obscene or indecent, and thus actionable under the Society's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to birth control literature
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1916 the NYSSV 'opposed Margaret Sanger and publishers of birth control books.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information about contraception was within the Society's scope of objectionable material, indicating moral/religious standards extended to sexual health information as well as erotica.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nudism or display of nudity could be prosecuted as indecent
rubrics_metrics.description: A bookseller was falsely arrested for displaying a book on 'nudism' in his store's window; Sumner was ordered to pay restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual or advertised nudity (even in a bookshop window) was treated as a potential violation of decency standards; the case also illustrates legal risk and later restitution for false arrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of depictions of violence and lawlessness in pulps
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1930 the NYSSV 'forced pulp publisher Harold Hersey to suppress the depiction of violence and lawlessness in his new line of gang pulps.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Society extended its remit to fiction that glamorized crime or violence, viewing such portrayals as socially harmful and subject to suppression or editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting of titillating fiction and nude photography ('girlie pulps')
rubrics_metrics.description: During the 1920s and '30s the Society prosecuted a 'long war' against 'girlie pulps' which featured 'titillating fiction, sometimes accompanied with nude photography.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material combining suggestive text and nude imagery was a distinct focus; enforcement included seizures and legal pressure on publishers and distributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling magazines as 'indecent' and seeking seizures/convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society attacked magazines as 'indecent' (examples: Artists and Models, Art Lovers' Magazine) and seized large numbers of magazines and books (e.g., '11,744 New Magazines Seized as Indecent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The indecency standard was applied to periodicals as well as books, with large-scale confiscations and prosecutions used as enforcement tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscene or offensive language as a ground for censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society attempted to block circulation of James T. Farrell's novel for 'using obscene language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rough or explicit language in fiction could be cited as indecent/obscene and used as a basis for legal or extralegal action against a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of literary expert testimony in obscenity trials
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1922 case (bookseller Raymond D. Halsey) 'established that literary experts could offer testimony in support of a book to guide the judge's opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes an evidentiary/procedural standard that affected how obscenity cases were tried — expert testimony about literary merit could be introduced to counter obscenity claims.
